titleStmt.title: Analysis of the diet of the long-snouted seahorse Hippocampus guttulatus by 18SrDNA amplification of prey in faeces

analytic.title: Analysis of the diet of the long-snouted seahorse Hippocampus guttulatus by 18SrDNA amplification of prey in faeces

div.p: Breeding in captivity for research or exhibition (e.g. in aquaria) can replace the capture of wild specimens of endangered species and allow controlled reinforcement of wild populations. With this aim, diet analysis and establishing the adequate prey are determinant factors for breeding success. However, non-invasive approaches such as faecal DNA analysis are advisable for analysing the diet of these species. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to demonstrate the usefulness of faecal DNA analysis by specific PCR amplification of prey DNA for assessing the diet of the seahorse Hippocampus guttulatus. In a comparison of the suitability of different genes (COI, 18SrRNA and 28SrRNA), 18SrRNA was found to be the most suitable for designing specific primers for the prey types fed to seahorses (Artemia, Palaemonetes and Mysidae). The technique was assessed in feeding experiments in which prey ingestion was recorded daily, and faeces were collected for DNA extraction and presence/absence PCR analysis. Amplification of the prey DNA in faeces was consistent with the sequence of prey supplied (prey eaten the day before was always detected). Differences in the time between feeding and detection in faeces suggested prey-specific gut passage times, which were shorter for Palaemonetes than for Mysidae. This fact highlights the importance of feeding trials to avoid overestimating the consumption of prey with long gut retention when PCR-based methods are used. This molecular technique is thus applicable for studying the feeding behaviour of captive seahorses and could be adapted for use in other marine species.

Seahorses (Hippocampus spp.) are an important patrimonial heritage of biodiversity and are considered a 'flagship' species for conservation programmes and marine-protected areas (Yasu e et al. 2012). The decline of many wild Hippocampus species represents a worldwide conservation challenge. All species of seahorses, including the European seahorses Hippocampus guttulatus and H. hippocampus, were on the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN 2012) in 1996 and in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) in 2004.

One approach for maintaining biodiversity and reducing the pressure on wild populations is captive breeding (Vincent et al. 2011), which can also be used for controlled reinforcement of wild populations in protected marine areas by adding individuals to an existing population of conspecifics (IUCN 1998). Feeding live prey also facilitates adaptation of species bred in captivity to the natural environment during restocking. Two determinants of successful breeding of a new marine fish species are identifying its nutritional requirements and establishing an adequate feeding regime based on live prey (Olivotto et al. 2011).
Captive animals should be fed on prey that are easy to maintain or cultivate and that fulfil the animals' nutritional

For example, H. guttulatus broodstock maintained at the Instituto de Investigaciones Marinas (IIM-CSIC) are fed enriched Artemia spp. (Planas et al. 2010), and their reproductive success is enhanced by feeding them captured wild shrimp (Palaemonetes varians or Mysidae) (Olivotto et al. 2011). Similar results were obtained with H. hippocampus (Otero-Ferrer et al. 2012). Assessments of prey suitability and feeding behaviour are based on analysis of the diet of wild seahorses in feeding experiments in captivity. The dietary composition and feeding behaviour of fish are usually established by morphological identification of prey remains in the gut. This method generally requires sacrifice of the fish, which should be avoided in the case of threatened or endangered species, such as seahorses. Use of PCR-based methods in trophic ecology studies has increased sharply over the past decade (Symondson 2002;King et al. 2008;Carre on-Mart ınez & Heath 2010;Maloy et al. 2011;Smith et al. 2011;Pompanon et al. 2012). The molecular approach provides accurate taxonomic resolution of prey (up to species level) and a short-term view of the diet, even when prey are degraded or when hard parts are lacking, which usually limits taxonomic determination in morphological analysis. Because of their high sensitivity, PCR-based methods can be applied to the detection of prey DNA in faeces (e.g. Corse et al. 2010).

The genes used most widely in molecular diet analysis are ribosomal (e.g. 18S, 28S) and mitochondrial genes (e.g. cytochrome oxidase I and II, cytochrome b) (King et al. 2008). These target genes have been chosen because of the availability of long sequences in databases such as Genbank (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/) and the Barcode of Life Database (http://www.barcodinglife.com/). They have also been used because of the strong probability that the loci will be amplified due to the high copy number in cells, either because ribosomal genes have multiple copies in the eukaryotic genome (Beebee & Rowe 2004) or because mitochondria are present in hundreds or thousands of copies in eukaryote cells (e.g. Hoy 2003). These arguments are valid for both nuclear ribosomal and mitochondrial genes. Thus, in the development of molecular methods for diet analysis, the suitability of the genes to be used should be based on other characteristics. For example, if a study requires fine taxonomic resolution of prey (e.g. genus or species), with a sequencing step, genes with greater discrimination will be required. A highly discriminant gene may, however, be problematic if a group-specific approach is used, because even close species may not have a common conservative region for designing group-specific primer. Comparative analysis should help in choosing the gene that optimizes the trade-off between informative sequences and the suitability for group-specific primer design.

Feeding trials with known ingested prey are also crucial in validating molecular techniques for prey detection (Sheppard et al. 2005;King et al. 2008;Roura et al. 2010; as shown by Carre on-Mart ınez & Heath 2010; Bowles et al. 2011;Maloy et al. 2011), andDeagle et al. (2005) showed that faecal analysis is useful for assessing gut passage of prey. Trials of feeding and gut passage should be performed with fasted specimens to ensure the absence of other prey in the gut (De Leon et al. 2006;Harper et al. 2006) and in a controlled environment that reproduces natural conditions (photoperiod, temperature) with controlled environmental parameters (Bromley 1994;Bochdansky & Deibel 2001). Prior knowledge of the prey ingested allows the detection of false-negative results, that is, failure of amplification when target DNA is present in the sample in feeding trials, as the prey is known to have been ingested. Moreover, detection of the DNA of a given prey in consecutive faecal samples after exclusive feeding on that prey is an indicator of the gut passage time of the prey, which is valuable for interpreting results and avoids overestimation of the consumption of prey with long retention in the gut.

Hippocampus guttulatus is a benthic fish associated with subtidal macrophytes, such as macroalgae (e.g. Sargassum, Cytoseira, Dictyota and Chondrus spp.) and seagrass (e.g. Zostera marina). The only published study on the natural diet of H. guttulatus was carried out in the Aegean Sea (Kitsos et al. 2008) and was based on morphological identification of prey from gut contents. The study showed that wild adults feed mainly on small crustaceans, such as Amphipoda, Anomura, Decapoda and Mysidae. There have been no published studies demonstrating the use of non-invasive approaches such as molecular analysis of faeces for determining the dietary composition and feeding behaviour of seahorses. The aim of this study was therefore to develop and validate a molecular protocol based on amplification of prey DNA from faeces in feeding trials with H. guttulatus. This will help to improve the rearing of seahorses providing a valuable tool for conservation (e.g. in controlled reinforcement of wild population in protected areas). Furthermore, by assessing the risk of false-negative results and evaluating the gut passage time of different prey, the protocol will be a reference for the interpretation of diet and feeding behaviour of wild populations. The method for faecal DNA analysis was developed for three prey species used at the IIM-CSIC in the breeding of H. guttulatus: P1, Mysidae; P2, P. varians; and P3, Artemia spp.

Wild Mysidacea were captured at Toralla (NW Spain, 42°12 0 6.64″N; 8°47 0 53.60″W) in an area where populations of the seahorses H. guttulatus and H. hippocampus are present (Valladares et al. 2013). As the captures always included Leptomysis spp. and Siriella spp., a mixture of these two species was given to the seahorses, referred to below as Mysidae. Grass shrimps (P. varians) were captured in natural ponds of the R ıa de Aveiro (Portugal, 40°38 0 0″N; 8°39 0 0″W), cultivated at the IIM-CSIC and fed on Artemia metanauplii and mussels. Adult Artemia spp. (EG, Inve, Spain) were cultured as described previously (Planas et al. 2013) and enriched with mixtures of the microalgae Phaeodactylum tricornutum and Isochrysis galbana, and one daily dose (0.1 g L À1 ) of red pepper (Bernaqua, Olen, Belgium) for at least 5 days.

Breeding H. guttulatus specimens were collected in 2010 by diving at two locations off the Galician coast (NW Spain): Bueu (42°19 0 54.06″N; 8°46 0 38.94″W) and Ald an (42°17 0 06.9″N; 8°49 0 59.3″W). Specimens were hand-caught, placed in 2-L plastic bags with surrounding water from the capture site and transported to the IIM-CSIC facilities in isothermal conditions.

Trials were conducted with adult H. guttulatus from the breeding stock maintained at the IIM-CSIC in ad hoc aquaria (Planas et al. 2008). The seawater temperature was maintained at 18 AE 0.5 °C, and the photoperiod was adapted to the natural day cycle. The salinity was 37 AE 2 g L À1 , and the pH was 8.0 AE 0.2.

Three males and three females of similar size (18.6 AE 0.8 and 16.8 mm AE 0.9 mm, respectively) and weight (24.6 AE 0.2 and 14.1 AE 0.8 g, respectively) were placed individually in six 30-L aquaria. All seahorses were fed simultaneously on a single prey or a mixture of the three prey, according to the following feeding sequence: P1 on day 1, P1 + P2 + P3 on day 3, P2 on day 5 and P3 on day 7. An equivalent dry weight biomass of all prey was sup-plied (71.5 AE 1.3 mg day À1 ), corresponding to 17 specimens of P1 (Mysidae), six specimens of P2 (P. varians) or 70 specimens of P3 (Artemia spp.), when a single-prey diet was supplied. In the mixed-prey diet on day 3, the dry weight corresponded to a mixture of 6 P1, 2 P2 and 24 P3. All prey were added daily at a single dose (at 10:00), except for P3, which were given in two feeds per day (at 10:00 and 14:00) because of the larger number of specimens supplied. Before the beginning of the experiment and on days 2, 4 and 6, between successive feeds with different prey, seahorses were starved for 24 h to ensure a completely empty gut (see Fig. 1). Uneaten prey from the previous experimental feeding day were removed from the aquaria at 09:00 and counted. The faeces produced in the aquaria were immediately collected by syphoning, and the collection time was recorded. Collected faeces were photographed with a digital camera. Prey samples and faeces were transferred to cryotubes containing 95°ethanol and stored at 4 °C for subsequent molecular analysis.

The molecular protocol followed the steps shown in Fig. 1, according to the approach described by Corse et al. (2010), based on total DNA extraction of faeces and amplification with prey-specific primers. In the first step, we developed a gene library to design specific primers. With the selected primers, we conducted molecular detection of prey in faeces of seahorses fed known prey types as described in the subsections below.

div.head: Development of prey gene library
div.p: A DNA sequence bank of the genes COI, 18SrDNA and 28SrDNA was developed for H. guttulatus and the three prey species. General PCR primers were used to obtain large gene fragments; then, PCR products were sequenced (see Data S1 for PCR conditions), and the sequences were aligned to evaluate the usefulness of each gene for designing prey-specific primers.

div.head: Selection of target gene
div.p: The suitability of genes for groupspecific primers is closely linked to the availability of preyspecific short oligonucleotide sequences. The complementary PCR primers of these genomic regions should amplify all the specimen of a given taxon and be unable to amplify DNA from specimens that do not belong to that taxon (Zarzoso-Lacoste et al. 2012). Therefore, the target gene was selected according to the abundance of genomic regions specific for each prey, whereas the specific taxonomic level was established as a function of the prey. In the case of Mysidae, a genomic region common to both Leptomysis and Siriella spp. was targeted; for Palaemonetes, a genomic region common to Decapoda was targeted. The aim was to develop primer that will be suitable for detecting the presence of these groups in the diet of wild individuals. Artemia spp. are used as a prey only in captive breeding, and therefore, a genusspecific region was targeted. A suitable gene should have regions with high mutation rates for genus-specific sequences and regions with lower mutation rates for higher taxon-specific sequences. We compared the suitability of the three genes for designing prey-specific primers and chose the gene with maximum heterogeneity of the mutation rate.

Design of specific primers A succession of three specific nucleotides at the 3 0 end of the primer sequence was considered sufficient for specific PCR. The primers were designed with Primer 3 software (Rozen & Skaletsky 2000) and Oligo Calculator 3.26 (Kibbe 2007). A minimum of 12 primer pairs per prey were then tested on the entire prey DNA bank as well as seahorse DNA to detect potential non-specific cross-amplification.

div.head: DNA extraction of faecal samples
div.p: Before DNA extraction from prey and faecal samples, the ethanol in which each sample had been stored was evaporated in a water bath at 55 °C.

Subsequently, the whole prey item or the whole faecal sample was subjected to DNA extraction with a Gentra Puregene Tissue Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), which has been used previously for DNA extraction of chitinous prey in fish faeces (Corse et al. 2010). All extractions were conducted in a room separate from those used for other steps. Water was used as a negative control to detect cross-contamination. The concentration and quality of the extraction products was verified by measuring (in triplicate) the A 260 /A 230 and A 260 /A 280 absorbance ratios with a Nanodrop 2000c (Ther-moScientific, Wilmington, DE, USA), as previous studies showed their relevance for explaining PCR performance for faecal samples (e.g. Zarzoso-Lacoste et al.

The percentage of fed prey that were ingested was checked by visual observation of the number of remaining prey individuals 24 h after feeding. When Mysidae specimens were supplied as a single prey type (day 1), 97% AE 5 of them were ingested. In four cases of six, all the prey supplied were ingested by the seahorses. In seahorses fed Palaemonetes alone (day 5), the average percentage of prey ingestion was 92% AE 9; three of six seahorses consumed 100% of the prey. For Artemia (day 7), 93% AE 13 of prey were ingested; five of six seahorses consumed all the prey. Of the mixed diet (day 3), all the Mysidae and Palaemonetes, but only 76% AE 31 of Artemia were ingested.

Faecal samples were collected in all the feeding trials. Most faeces (71%) were found the day after feeding (days 2, 4, 6 and 8) (list of faecal sampling in Data S2); in other cases, faeces from a single feed were released over 2 days (e.g. days 3, 5, 7 and 9), and the results for faecal samples that corresponded to the same feeding event were compiled for clarity (Table 2).

Observation of the faeces under a binocular lens showed different degrees of prey digestion. For example, in the fae-ces composed of Palaemonetes, undigested parts of the carapace were observed (Fig. 2).

For each gene, the prey bank library comprised the two Mysidae taxa, Leptomysis spp. (Genbank accession number of COI: KC763187, of 28S: KC763185, of 18S: KC763182) and Siriella spp. (28S: KC763186 and 18S: KC763181), the sequence of P. varians (COI: KC763188, and 18S: KC763180) and the sequence of Artemia spp. (28S: KC763184 and 18S: KC763183). Genbank sequences were chosen to complete the three missing sequences when PCR failed to amplify the gene. (More details about these sequences are given in the legends to the Data S3.)

Alignment of 28S sequences revealed greater evolutionary distances between species than in 18S or COI alignments (see Data S3). Moreover, the mutation rate differed by gene, COI alignment showing a homogeneous mutation rate (mainly restricted to the third position of the codon) and the ribosomal genes (18SrDNA and 28SrDNA) showing a heterogeneous mutation rate due to the alternation between hypervariable regions surrounded by more or less conserved regions (illustrated in Data S4).

The suitability of COI, 18SrDNA and 28SrDNA genes for detecting prey-specific DNA short sequences was compared by assessing the presence of specific regions for the design of group-specific primers. High divergence between sequences in both COI and 28S alignments made it difficult to detect regions that were conserved in both Mysidae taxa but were specific to that group and not to the other prey (P. varians and Artemia spp.). In contrast, 18S alignment offered possibilities for designing group-specific primers because of the availability of numerous regions displaying the required taxonomic specificity for Mysidae. Moreover, the larger size of the 18SrDNA gene (1800 bp) than the region commonly available for 28SrDNA (900 bp) and COI (600 bp) facilitated the finding of specific regions. Thus, 18SrDNA was chosen as the target gene.

A total of 30 specific primer sets were designed (see Data S5), making it possible to test 44 primers (17 targeted P1, 12 targeted P2 and 15 targeted P3). Electrophoresis of PCR products led to the exclusion of some primers, principally because of PCR failure or migration of the corresponding PCR products into multiband profiles. In the retained primer set, we systematically selected one that amplified the shorter amplicon (Table 1), as the probability of detecting target DNA on a degraded DNA matrix (due to the digestive process) is enhanced by minimizing the amplicon size (Zaidi et al. 1999;Deagle et al. 2006;Sint et al. 2011).

The quality of DNA extraction was reasonable, and the PCR results were robust. Three quarters of the A 260 /A 230 2. For 31 faecal samples and three prey-specific primer sets, 54 amplifications succeeded, showing strong repeatability of PCR replicates (4/4), except for four PCRs for which the repeatability varied between 1/4 and 3/4. The DNA of at least one prey species was detected in all faecal samples except one (97% PCR success rate), which was the sample containing the lowest DNA concentration (6 ng ll À1 for specimen M N81 at day 3; see Data S2).

div.p: DNA of the prey species that had been fed was detected consistently in faeces 24 h after feeding. Surprisingly, Art-emia DNA was also detected 24 h after feeding with Palaemonetes and on day 2 in the faeces of one seahorse (F N89) fed wild Mysidae. Palaemonetes DNA was not detected in faeces 48 h after feeding, and use of another Palaemonetes-specific primer set confirmed this result (data not shown). In contrast, Mysidae DNA was detected in faeces 72 h after feeding in 50% of cases.

To confirm the specificity of the primer pairs, 18 randomly chosen PCR products (6 per specific primer set) were sequenced by GATC Biotech (Cologne, Germany). The BLAST on Genbank allowed identification of the sequences obtained with the Mysidae-and Artemia-specific primer set with high confidence (E-value, <E-10). Furthermore, the BLAST results showed that both Mysidae taxa were amplified (see more details in Data S6). For the amplicons obtained with the Palaemonetes-specific primer set, the corresponding sequences showed identical Max scores for numerous Genbank sequences belonging to Decapoda.

The molecular protocol for analysing the diet of H. guttulatus developed in this study includes (i) the design of preyspecific primers targeting 18SrDNA, (ii) verification of effective prey DNA extraction from the predator faecal matrix with successful PCR amplification, and (iii) validation in adequate feeding trials with the three targeted preys.

The choice of the target gene is critical in developing molecular methods for diet analysis, which should be guided by the required taxonomic level for prey identification. In this study, we developed specific discriminative primers for the three prey, with the added constraint that primers for Mysidae amplify both Leptomysis and Siriella.

COI genes generally have a higher mutation rate than nuclear genes (Brown et al. 1979;L opez et al. 1997;Ballard 2000;Mueller 2006), decreasing the percentage sequence similarity between species. In our case, sequences in COI revealed high divergence, which made it difficult to find specific regions common to the two Mysidae taxa but discriminatory for the other two prey and for the predator. Furthermore, the mutation rate among the COI in our target species was found to be homogeneous, with mutations mainly found every third codon (i.e. favouring synonymous mutations). This made it difficult to design a species-specific primer with this gene (Harper et al. 2005, Harper et al. 2006;Admassu et al. 2006) and hampered the search of specific regions for both Mysidae taxa (see Data S4). Ribosomal genes are not protein-coding genes, and the mutation rate is heterogeneous, with alternation of hypervariable regions and more or less conserved regions, depending on the taxa (see Crease & Colbourne 1998for crustaceans, and Wuyts et al. 2001, 2002 for other Eukaryota). The mutation rate is structured by loop regions and functional regions, which can be viewed in the secondary structure of the ribosomal subunit (e.g. for 18S see Wuyts et al. 2001). In our case, the 28SrDNA gene showed high divergence between sequences, and specific regions for both Mysidae species were rare. However, Conserved regions were more frequent in 18SrRNA, allowing for the design of group-specific primers.

div.p: Ribosomal genes are generally more suitable than COI for detecting micro-organisms in the digestive system (e.g. 16SrRNA for bacterial flora, Matsuki et al. 2002;Baker et al. 2003) and are often preferred for designing groupspecific primers for prey detection in diet analysis (e.g. Dodd 2004;Vences et al. 2005). The reason commonly advanced is that ribosomal genes have a lower mutation rate than COI (e.g. discussed by Corse et al. 2013), enhancing the likelihood of specific regions (King et al. 2008). As we argue in this paper, this is due mainly to mutation rate dynamics, which are heterogeneous in ribosomal genes and homogeneous in protein-coding genes. In ribosomal genes, the mutation rate depends on the region, with higher rates in less conserved regions. In 18SrDNA, species-specific primers can be designed in regions with high mutation rates (Ward & Adams 1998), and familyspecific (Corse et al. 2010) or 'universal' primers (Miquelis et al. 2000) can be designed in regions with lower mutation rates.

Group-specific primers (e.g. for Mysidae and Decapoda) are more suitable for establishing predominant groups in trophic ecological studies of species with a wide range of prey, such as wild seahorses, than highly accurate prey determination (e.g. genus or species level). In this study, the three group-specific primer sets targeted different taxonomic levels. Mysidae primers targeted an 18SrDNA region for both taxa, Leptomysis and Siriella, which are commonly present in the habitat of seahorses and are potentially part of their diet. For Palaemonetes, we targeted a highly conserved region for Decapoda, so the primers will be suitable for detecting not only Palaemonetes in feeding trials (as no other Decapoda were used) but also the presence of Decapoda in the diet of wild individuals. For Artemia, which are not prey for seahorses in nature, the primers used were specific to that genus, as Artemia will have to be detected only in feeding trials in captivity.

Our study illustrates the trade-off that must be made in the choice of target locus and the desired taxonomic information in analysis of prey in faecal DNA. In general, we have established that in dietary studies in which highly accurate prey determination (e.g. species taxonomy) and sequencing of amplicons are required, COI is the most suitable gene (Ratnasingham & Herbert 2007;Meusnier et al. 2008). In a study that requires a higher taxonomic level (like the present study), group-specific primers can be used, and 18SrDNA is recommended.

The DNA extraction kit used in this study satisfied the quality level required for DNA-based analysis of H. guttulatus faeces. Although the mean values of A 260 /A 280 were within the range indicated by the manufacturer to prevent PCR trouble-shooting, the low A 260 /A 230 mean value would suggest that contaminants (e.g. salts or organic compounds such as peptides) were co-purified. Because of the digestion process, a low prey DNA concentration coupled with PCR inhibitors in faeces can increase the risk for false-negative results (failure of amplification when target DNA is present in the sample), which may bias diet interpretation (Deagle et al. 2005;King et al. 2008). However, the PCR success rate and the results of the reproducibility tests suggest that co-purified contaminants had a limited impact on PCR efficiency and that a purification step (e.g. with QIAGEN spin columns that eliminate co-extracted products), which might reduce the DNA concentration, is unnecessary. In only one case did faecal extraction fail to amplify at least one prey (M N81 on day 3), probably due to a low DNA concentration.

Systematic detection in faeces of the prey ingested the previous day, together with the PCR success rate, validate the accuracy of the protocol. If false-negative result bias had been important, inconsistency between the feeding trials and molecular detection or a weak PCR success rate would have been expected (Deagle et al. 2005). Our results show that the protocol allows the detection in faeces of ingested prey and the detection of prey in successive faeces varying by type of prey. For example, Mysidae were detectable in faeces up to 3 days after feeding in 50% of cases, while Palaemonetes was not detected after 2 days. Feeding trials with known prey or with selected representatives of potential prey groups allow comparisons of preyspecific gut passage or retention time and can indicate potential biases in the analysis of faeces from wild specimens (Beukers-Stewart & Jones 2004). Numerous studies of animals in captivity show that the sensitivity of molecular approaches offers an opportunity to monitor the gut passage of prey (Tollit et al. 2003;Deagle et al. 2005;Sheppard et al. 2005;Greenstone et al. 2007;Hosseini et al. 2008;Dunshea 2009;Oehm et al. 2011). As the feeding trials in our study were conducted with equivalent daily feeding ratios (dry weight) of prey, and the daily meals were fully consumed in most cases, the results reflect preyspecific differences in gut passage time. Such heterogeneous passage time may be a source of misinterpretation in prey analysis, as the frequency of detection of prey may be influenced by its retention time in the gut. For example, the consumption of a prey with a long gut retention time may be overestimated in relation to other prey with shorter passage times. Assessing differences in the passage time of different types of prey and understanding the causes should help to prevent such misinterpretation for studying wild specimens.

Gut passage time in fish is influenced by several environmental parameters, such as temperature (Bromley 1994;Bochdansky & Deibel 2001), meal size (Windell 1967;Bagge 1977;Dos Santos & Jobling 1995;Andersen 1998) and the intrinsic characteristics of the prey, such as size (e.g. Adams & Breck 1990), energy density (e.g. Windell & Norris 1969;Grove et al. 1978;Dos Santos & Jobling 1988) and digestibility (e.g. Berens & Murie 2008).

In seahorses, the temperate species H. guttulatus has a longer gut passage time than the tropical species Hippocampus kuda. In 6-month-old juvenile H. kuda fed a mixture of Artemia nauplii and Mysids, Tanu et al. (2012) observed complete clearance by gut dissection after 24-h starvation. In our study, the gut of adult H. guttulatus was not completely empty after 24 h, and ingested prey were still detectable in faeces 2-3 days later. This difference may be due not only to the species but also to the culture temperature (18 °C for H. guttulatus and 27 °C for H. kuda), which inversely correlates with gut passage time (Bromley 1994).

Prey size is often negatively correlated with gut passage rate (e.g. Mills et al. 1984;He & Wurtsbaugh 1993), although this finding should not be generalized; for example, Andersen (1999) did not observed an effect of size on gut passage time in Merlangius merlangus and reported that the energy density and biochemical composition of prey had a greater effect. With regard to the influence of prey digestibility, it was shown in yellow rockfish Sebastes chrysomelas fed on Percomorpha spp. that the crustacean exoskeleton remains longer in the fish gut than prey containing fewer indigestible hard parts (such as fish) (Hopkins & Larson 1990). In that study, it was hypothesized that enzymatic attack on the prey in the gut would be delayed due to the chitinous exoskeleton of the crustacean. The reported gut passage time of crustaceans by fish is especially heterogeneous (Tyler 1970;MacDonald et al. 1982;Dos Santos & Jobling 1995;Andersen 1999;Berens 2005), probably due to wide variation in the exoskeleton structure of different crustacean species (Bobelmann et al. 2007). In vendace (Coregonus albula) and whitefish (Coregonus lavaretus) larvae, Sutela & Huusko (2000) observed that hardbodied zooplankton (e.g. Bosmina and Daphnia spp.) was evenly distributed in the fish gut, whereas soft-bodied prey (e.g. Synchaeta and Polyarthra spp.) were concentrated in the first quarter of the gut. These studies illustrate the possible relationship between gut passage and digestibility of prey, by morphological analysis of the remaining hard parts. Although the sensitivity of the molecular methods may be different, it is likely that the presence of prey DNA in consecutive faeces also correlates with prey digestibility.

In this study, the larger prey Palaemonetes was detected for a shorter time in faeces than smaller prey, such as Mysidae. In addition, the presence of remains of Palaemonetes in faeces (Fig. 2) suggests that the exoskeleton of this prey type is poorly digestible. Mechanical structures to break down the chitinaceous exoskeletons of crustaceans are lacking in seahorses, which suck and swallow the entire prey through a simple intestinal tract with no stomach (Bergert & Wainwright 1997;Lin et al. 2007;Tanu et al. 2012). The absence of a specialized structure in the gut to permit retention of a food bolus might explain the negative correlation between prey size and prey passage time in Hippocampus. Moreover, for equal daily meals, larger prey present a smaller surface for enzymatic digestion. Unfortunately, there are no published data on digestive enzymatic activity in seahorses or other Syngnathids. A recent study of bacteria associated with the intestinal tract of H. kuda mentions characterization of bacterial extracellular enzymes, which may play a role in digestion (Tanu et al. 2012). Strong endogenous chitinase activity has been detected in fish such as rainbow trout (Lindsay et al. 1984) and cobia larvae (Fines & Holt 2010), in which there are no mechanical structures to break down the chitinous exoskeletons of crustacean prey. Further study is needed of the biochemistry and digestibility of prey and of the digestive enzymatic equipment (chitinases, proteases, lipases and carbohydrases) in H. guttulatus.

Owing to differential gut passage times, the faecal DNA matrix on any given day might reflect a number of feeding events over several days, emphasizing the need to define an adequate time frame for molecular analysis. In the present study, the temporal frame of molecular analysis in faeces ranged from 24 h (prey were always detected the day after their ingestion) to 72 h (Mysidae were detected up to 3 days after their ingestion). These results indicate that molecular analysis of faeces collected from wild seahorses reflects at least the past 72 h of feeding activity. In some seahorses that fed exclusively on Mysidae, Artemia DNA was detected in faeces released 24 h later (day 2; Table 2). As the Mysidae fed in this study were captured in the wild, they would not have Artemia in their gut. Therefore, it is feasible that Artemia DNA detected in faeces of the seahorses fed Mysidae represented residuals of Artemia fed 48 h previously, implying that prey can remain for 48 h in the gut and that 24 h of fasting is insufficient to ensure gut emptiness. Palaemonetes are also cultivated by a continuous supply of Artemia, and detection of Artemia in faeces of seahorses collected 24 h after feeding with Palemonetes (day 6) would also be due to secondary predation rather than the remains of primary consumption of Artemia (day 3).

Secondary predation occurs when a primary predator that has consumed the target prey is consumed by a second predator (or scavenger), in which the remains of the target prey are found (modified from Harwood et al. 2001). Numerous studies have shown the reliability of PCR-based methods for detecting such indirect predation using faecal DNA analysis. For example, DNA of aphids ingested by spiders was detected in the digestive tract of carabids (Sheppard et al. 2005). In contrast, et al. (2008) found potential sources of error in analyses of the diet of arthropods due to the detection of prey DNA after secondary cannibalistic and intraguild predation. Both of these studies were conducted by molecular analysis of gut contents, and, to the best of our knowledge, there are no published results on secondary predation detection in faeces of vertebrates. Secondary predation must be systematically considered to avoid false interpretation of trophic web chains (King et al. 2008). Detection of secondary predation by DNA-based methods depends on the time between ingestion of a given prey by a second prey and ingestion of the second prey by the predator. In carabids fed on spiders, Sheppard et al. (2005) detected secondary predation 20 h after ingestion of their last food, when spiders were ingested immediately after aphid consumption. The time decreased significantly (a few hours) when spiders were ingested by carabids 4 h after aphid consumption. Such studies highlight the influence of the time between the two predation events on the detection of secondary predation. In our case, the time between the ingestion of Artemia by Palaemonetes and the ingestion of Palaemonetes by Artemia was not long enough to prevent secondary predation, indicating the need for longer prey starvation in future feeding trials. Feeding trials limited to a few prey-predator interactions should be reliable for assessing the time frame of prey-predator ingestion. In more complex systems such as seahorses in nature, however, where they have a wide prey spectrum, capturing and analysing samples of the potential prey in the habitat of the predator should be the alternative to assessing secondary predation.

The agreement between the results for ingested prey and DNA analysis of faeces shows that the molecular protocol developed in this study ensures correct identification of prey fed to H. guttulatus, with no false-negative results. The method is useful for monitoring the gut passage time of prey and shows that the gut passage time of crustaceans in Hippocampus is species-dependent, probably due to differences in their digestibility and the enzymatic activity in the stomach-less gut of seahorses. Furthermore, the method is sensitive for detecting secondary predation among experimental prey. Both differential gut passage time and secondary predation should be considered to avoid misinterpretation of food regimes in wild specimens.

Hence, the technique could be used in further studies of feeding in captivity and could be adapted for studies in the wild. For example, as H. guttulatus forage mainly on crustaceans, the use of order (e.g. Decapoda)-or family (e.g. Mysidae)-specific primers within the Crustacea subphylum should be sufficiently informative for studying the feeding behaviour of this species. Coupling this strategy with nextgeneration sequencing, including a method to inhibit amplification of predator DNA (e.g. use of a selective blocking primer, Vestheim & Jarman 2008), should significantly increase the resolution of diet analysis. Nevertheless, in both cases, it will be essential to build a bank of prey from the seahorse habitat to apply the molecular approach to wild specimens. Furthermore, knowledge of the biochemical composition of the prey and their digestibility by predators would provide a better understanding of predator-prey interactions.

The PCR success rate was evaluated by dividing the number of faeces samples in which a minimum of one of the three prey types was detected by the total number of faecal samples. Randomly chosen PCR amplicons obtained from faecal DNA extractions were sequenced to validate correct targeting of the prey-specific primer set. Each sequence was determined by megaBLAST against the nucleotide (nr/nt) database of Genbank. In this step, 'Max score', which characterizes the score of alignments, and the 'E-value', which reflects their significance(Korf et al. 2003) [both parameters available in the NCBI BLAST result interface website (http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)], were considered. We decided that the sequence with the best Max score corresponded to the closest sequence available on Genbank with a maximal threshold of the E-value fixed at E-10. In cases in which equal Max scores were obtained with different Genbank sequences, we attributed the query sequence to the lowest taxonomic level containing all the corresponding species.
